# Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7? {#sec-calibration}

**45 minutes · work individually**

::: {.callout-important}
## A suggested addition, not part of the original module
This exercise was proposed and drafted by the assistant that rebuilt the
booklet, not ported from an earlier version of the module. Exercise 4.3 names calibration as something it has not checked and cannot claim, and the booklet never returns to it. A probability used to make a decision is worth nothing unless it means what it says. Treat it as a
draft to accept, rewrite or delete: nothing else depends on it, and removing it
means deleting this file and its line in `_quarto.yml`.
:::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Build a calibration table by hand — bin the predicted probabilities, and put
  the mean prediction in each bin next to the rate actually observed in it.
- Say why a model can be perfectly ranked and badly calibrated, and name a
  metric that notices the difference.
- Decide whether a gap between predicted and observed is a fault in the model
  or the size of the test set.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-thresholds chose a threshold of 0.17 from a cost ratio of five to one, and
the arithmetic behind that choice assumed something it never checked: that a
predicted probability of 0.17 belongs to a group of patients of whom about 17%
really do have diabetes. If the probabilities are on a different scale from the
events, the threshold is still a number but it is no longer the number the cost
ratio implies.

That assumption has a name. A model is **calibrated** when, among the patients
it gives probability $q$, the long-run proportion with the outcome is $q$.
Calibration is a property of the probabilities themselves, and it is not
measured by anything Day 4 has computed so far: accuracy, sensitivity and
specificity all throw the probability away at the threshold and look only at
the classes that come out.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## One number borrowed from Day 5
Task 3 needs the area under the ROC curve, which is @sec-classification-metrics
and has not been taught yet. You need only one fact about it here: AUC is the
probability that a randomly chosen positive patient is given a higher score than
a randomly chosen negative one. It is a statement about **order** and nothing
else. That is the whole point of Task 3, and you can take the number on trust
until Day 5 explains it.
:::

## Worked example — calibration in the large, and where it stops holding

Same model and same split as @sec-thresholds: `diabetes ~ glucose`, fitted to
615 patients, scored on the 153 held back.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = train)

p_train <- predict(fit, train, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
p_logit <- predict(fit, test,  type = "prob")$.pred_pos

source("checks/checks.R")
cat("on the training rows\n")
check_probabilities(p_train, prevalence = mean(train$diabetes == "pos"))
cat("on the held-out rows\n")
check_probabilities(p_logit, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"]  == "pos").astype(int)

fit = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(train[["glucose"]], y_train)
p_train = fit.predict_proba(train[["glucose"]])[:, 1]
p_logit = fit.predict_proba(test[["glucose"]])[:, 1]

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
print("on the training rows")
check_probabilities(p_train, prevalence=float(y_train.mean()))
print("on the held-out rows")
check_probabilities(p_logit, prevalence=float(y_test.mean()))
```
:::

The first check passes to six decimal places and it could not have done anything
else: @sec-logistic-regression showed that a logistic regression with an
intercept makes the mean of its fitted probabilities equal the observed
prevalence, exactly, on the rows it was fitted to. That is an algebraic identity,
not evidence.

The second check reports `[fix]`. The mean predicted probability on the held-out
patients is 0.386, the prevalence among them is 0.359, and the gap of 0.027 is
larger than the check's tolerance of 0.02. Nothing is broken: the training
prevalence is 0.366 and the test prevalence is 0.359, so the model is carrying
the training rate onto a test set that happens to be slightly healthier. This is
the weakest possible calibration claim — **calibration in the large**, one number
against one number — and the model already misses it by two and a half
percentage points on 153 patients.

A model can pass that test and still be useless, because it averages. A model
that gave every patient 0.359 would pass it perfectly.

## Task 1 — The calibration curve, before a package draws one

Split the predicted probabilities into five bins of width 0.2. In each bin,
count the patients, average the predictions, and compute the proportion who
actually had diabetes. A calibrated model puts those last two columns on top of
each other.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

calibration_table <- function(p, truth, n_bins = 5) {
  edges <- seq(0, 1, length.out = ______ + 1)
  tibble(bin      = cut(p, breaks = edges, include.lowest = TRUE),
         p        = p,
         observed = as.integer(truth == "pos")) |>
    group_by(bin, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n              = n(),
              mean_predicted = mean(p),
              observed_rate  = mean(______),
              .groups = "drop")
}

logit_cal <- calibration_table(p_logit, test$diabetes)
logit_cal

gap_logit <- max(abs(logit_cal$mean_predicted - logit_cal$observed_rate), na.rm = TRUE)
check_metric_range(gap_logit, 0, 0.35, "largest predicted-minus-observed gap")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

def calibration_table(p, truth, n_bins=5):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    bin_id = np.minimum((p * ______).astype(int), n_bins - 1)
    out = pd.DataFrame({"bin": bin_id, "p": p, "observed": np.asarray(truth)})
    return (out.groupby("bin")
               .agg(n=("p", "size"), mean_predicted=("p", "mean"),
                    observed_rate=("______", "mean"))
               .reindex(range(n_bins)))

logit_cal = calibration_table(p_logit, y_test)
print(logit_cal.round(4))

gap_logit = (logit_cal["mean_predicted"] - logit_cal["observed_rate"]).abs().max()
check_metric_range(gap_logit, 0, 0.35, "largest predicted-minus-observed gap")
```

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")

def calibration_table(p, truth, n_bins=5):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)

    out = pd.DataFrame({"bin": bin_id, "p": p, "observed": np.asarray(truth)})

               .agg(n=("p", "size"), mean_predicted=("p", "mean"),

               .reindex(range(n_bins)))

logit_cal = calibration_table(p_logit, y_test)

gap_logit = (logit_cal["mean_predicted"] - logit_cal["observed_rate"]).abs().max()
check_metric_range(gap_logit, 0, 0.35, "largest predicted-minus-observed gap")

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The bins are five equal slices of the interval from 0 to 1. In R one function
turns a numeric vector into a factor of intervals; in Python multiplying by the
number of bins and truncating does the same job, with the top edge needing care
because a probability of exactly 1 would otherwise fall into a sixth bin.
:::

Both languages give the same five rows, because the split and the model are
fixed:

| Bin | Patients | Mean predicted | Observed rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0–0.2 | 40 | 0.146 | 0.125 |
| 0.2–0.4 | 57 | 0.297 | 0.298 |
| 0.4–0.6 | 23 | 0.474 | 0.522 |
| 0.6–0.8 | 17 | 0.703 | 0.647 |
| 0.8–1.0 | 16 | 0.842 | 0.625 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,20,29,29]"}

The middle of the range is close. The top bin is not: the model promises 0.84
and delivers 0.63, which in a clinic is the difference between "almost certainly"
and "probably". The largest gap is 0.217.

## Is that top bin a fault, or is it sixteen patients?

Before reading anything into a gap, ask what gap you would see from a model that
was *perfectly* calibrated. We can answer that exactly, because we can generate
outcomes from the model's own probabilities and rebuild the table. This reuses
the `calibration_table()` you wrote in Task 1, so run that cell first.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
set.seed(1)
max_gap <- function(y) {
  tab <- calibration_table(p_logit, factor(ifelse(y == 1, "pos", "neg"),
                                           levels = c("neg", "pos")))
  max(abs(tab$mean_predicted - tab$observed_rate), na.rm = TRUE)
}
simulated <- replicate(2000, max_gap(rbinom(length(p_logit), 1, p_logit)))

round(c(observed      = max_gap(as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos")),
        sim_median    = median(simulated),
        sim_90th      = unname(quantile(simulated, 0.90)),
        p_value       = mean(simulated >= max_gap(as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos")))), 3)
```

## Python

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def max_gap(y):
    tab = calibration_table(p_logit, y)
    return float((tab["mean_predicted"] - tab["observed_rate"]).abs().max())

observed = max_gap(y_test.to_numpy())
simulated = np.array([max_gap(rng.binomial(1, p_logit)) for _ in range(2000)])

{"observed": round(observed, 3),
 "sim_median": round(float(np.median(simulated)), 3),
 "sim_90th": round(float(np.quantile(simulated, 0.90)), 3),
 "p_value": round(float((simulated >= observed).mean()), 3)}
```
:::

A perfectly calibrated model on 153 patients in five bins produces a largest gap
of 0.126 on a typical run, and exceeds the 0.217 we measured in about 12% of
runs. The curve is not evidence that this model is miscalibrated. It is
mostly evidence that sixteen patients is not many, and it is the reason
calibration plots in papers should carry the bin counts — which is why
`calibration_table()` returns `n` first.

## Task 2 — A second model, on the same patients

@sec-random-forest grows 500 trees and averages their votes, and averages of
bounded numbers are pulled towards the middle. The standard warning is that an
untouched random forest is poorly calibrated: too timid near 0 and near 1. Fit
the Day 5.4 specification to **these** training rows, build its calibration
table, and draw both curves against the diagonal.

The forest sees all eight predictors and the logistic regression sees one, so
this is not a fair comparison of accuracy. It is a comparison of the shape of
two curves, which is what the plot is for.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
library(ggplot2)
source("checks/checks.R")

set.seed(123)
rf <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

p_rf <- predict(rf, test, type = "prob")$______
check_probabilities(p_rf, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))

curves <- bind_rows(
  calibration_table(p_logit, test$diabetes) |> mutate(model = "logistic, glucose only"),
  calibration_table(p_rf,    test$diabetes) |> mutate(model = "random forest, 8 predictors")
) |> filter(n > 0)

ggplot(curves, aes(x = mean_predicted, y = ______, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted probability in the bin",
       y = "Observed rate in the bin", colour = NULL, size = "patients")
```

## Stuck?
The forest's probability column has the same name as the logistic regression's,
because `parsnip` names it after the factor level; in Python `predict_proba`
again returns one column per class in `classes_` order. The second blank is the
column of `calibration_table()` that holds what actually happened.
:::

The warning does not come true here, and that is worth more than if it had. The
forest's probabilities reach both ends of the interval — 0.008 to 0.906 in R,
0.004 to 0.924 in Python — rather than huddling near the
prevalence, its mean is 0.362 against a prevalence of 0.359 — it passes the
check the logistic regression failed — and its largest bin gap is 0.19 in R and
0.30 in Python. Neither model is distinguishable from calibrated at this sample
size, and the two languages disagree about which looks worse, which tells you
how much signal there is in the comparison.

Pile-up towards the middle is real, but it is a property of small or heavily
regularised ensembles. Five hundred unrestricted trees on 615 patients are
confident enough to reach both ends.

## Task 3 — Same order, different numbers

Now break the probabilities on purpose, in a way no ranking metric can see.
Shrink every prediction a third of the way towards 0.5:

$$q = 0.5 + \frac{p - 0.5}{3}.$$

This is strictly increasing in $p$, so the patients come out in exactly the same
order. Compute the AUC before and after, and the calibration table after.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
p_squashed <- 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / ______

auc_raw      <- roc_auc_vec(test$diabetes, p_logit,     event_level = "second")
auc_squashed <- roc_auc_vec(test$diabetes, ______, event_level = "second")
check_matches(auc_squashed, auc_raw, tol = 1e-4, label = "AUC after squashing")

brier <- function(p) mean((p - as.integer(test$diabetes == "pos"))^2)
round(c(auc_raw = auc_raw, auc_squashed = auc_squashed,
        brier_raw = brier(p_logit), brier_squashed = brier(p_squashed)), 6)

check_probabilities(p_squashed, prevalence = mean(test$diabetes == "pos"))
calibration_table(p_squashed, test$diabetes)
```

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

p_squashed = 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / 3

auc_raw      = roc_auc_score(y_test, p_logit)
auc_squashed = roc_auc_score(y_test, p_squashed)
check_matches(auc_squashed, auc_raw, tol=1e-4, label="AUC after squashing")

print({"auc_raw": round(auc_raw, 6), "auc_squashed": round(auc_squashed, 6),
       "brier_raw": round(brier_score_loss(y_test, p_logit), 6),
       "brier_squashed": round(brier_score_loss(y_test, p_squashed), 6)})

check_probabilities(p_squashed, prevalence=float(y_test.mean()))
print(calibration_table(p_squashed, y_test).round(4))
```
:::
:::
:::

The **Brier score** in that cell is the mean squared difference between the
probability and the outcome coded 0 or 1. Unlike AUC it is a *proper* scoring
rule: it is minimised by telling the truth, so it falls when the ranking improves
and also when the numbers themselves get closer to the events.

## The result that should bother you

The squashed model and the original model are the same model. One is a
one-line transformation of the other, and every patient keeps their position in
the queue.

1. The AUC is 0.742022 before and 0.742022 after — identical to six decimal
   places, in both languages, because AUC counts pairs in the right order and
   the order did not change. A report that quotes only AUC cannot tell these two
   models apart, and most published model reports quote only AUC.
2. The Brier score rises from 0.199 to 0.218, and the probabilities now span
   0.359 to 0.625. Every patient is told something between "a bit more likely
   than not to be fine" and "not far off even odds", which is a model with
   nothing to say.
3. Apply @sec-thresholds' cost-minimising threshold of 0.17 to each. The
   original probabilities send 123 of the 153 patients for investigation at a
   cost of 74. The squashed probabilities send **all 153**, at a cost of 98 —
   exactly the cost of ignoring the model and investigating everybody. The
   entire value Day 4.3 extracted from this model has been destroyed by a
   transformation that AUC says never happened.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
cost_of <- function(p, threshold, cost_fn = 5, cost_fp = 1) {
  called_pos <- p >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- test$diabetes == "pos"
  cost_fn * sum(!called_pos & truly_pos) + cost_fp * sum(called_pos & !truly_pos)
}
p_squashed <- 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / 3

for (threshold in c(0.17, 0.5)) {
  print(rbind(
    raw      = c(threshold = threshold, n_investigated = sum(p_logit    >= threshold),
                 cost = cost_of(p_logit,    threshold)),
    squashed = c(threshold = threshold, n_investigated = sum(p_squashed >= threshold),
                 cost = cost_of(p_squashed, threshold))))
}
```

## Python

```{python}
truly_pos = y_test.to_numpy() == 1
p_squashed = 0.5 + (p_logit - 0.5) / 3

def cost_of(p, threshold, cost_fn=5, cost_fp=1):
    called_pos = p >= threshold
    return int(cost_fn * (~called_pos & truly_pos).sum()
               + cost_fp * (called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())

pd.DataFrame([
    dict(model=name, threshold=t, n_investigated=int((p >= t).sum()), cost=cost_of(p, t))
    for t in (0.17, 0.5)
    for name, p in [("raw", p_logit), ("squashed", p_squashed)]
])
```
:::

The sting is in the two rows for 0.5. At that threshold the two
models are indistinguishable — both call 40 patients positive and both cost 165
— because 0.5 is the one point this transformation leaves alone. A team that
had never moved off the default would have found nothing wrong, and would have
been right that nothing was wrong *for them*. Calibration starts to matter the
moment the threshold stops being arbitrary.

## Reflection

1. AUC did not move and the Brier score did. Write the one-sentence rule you
   would give a colleague for when AUC alone is an adequate summary of a
   clinical prediction model, and when it is not.
2. The noise simulation said we cannot tell this model from a calibrated one on
   153 patients. How many patients would you want before you were willing to
   publish a calibration curve with five bins, and what would you report
   alongside it if you could not get them?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (the data is synthetic; forests move the last digit).

| | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| mean predicted, training rows / prevalence | 0.365854 / 0.365854 | 0.365854 / 0.365854 |
| mean predicted, test rows / prevalence | 0.386 / 0.359 | 0.386 / 0.359 |
| logistic: largest bin gap | 0.217 | 0.217 |
| logistic: AUC / Brier | 0.742022 / 0.199 | 0.742022 / 0.199 |
| simulated largest gap: median, 90th, p | 0.126, 0.217, 0.12 | 0.126, 0.217, 0.12 |
| forest: mean predicted, range | 0.362, 0.008–0.906 | 0.362, 0.004–0.924 |
| forest: AUC / Brier / largest gap | 0.755 / 0.192 / 0.19 | 0.743 / 0.197 / 0.30 |
| squashed: AUC / Brier / range | 0.742022 / 0.218 / 0.359–0.625 | same |
| cost at 0.17: raw, squashed | 74, 98 | 74, 98 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[46,27,27]"}

**Answers.** (1) AUC is adequate when the output is a ranked list and a fixed
number of people will be seen — a waiting list, a recall quota — because only
order is used. It is inadequate the moment a probability is compared with a
number: a threshold from a cost ratio, a risk communicated to a patient, a
prediction combined with another model's. (2) There is no single right answer
and the useful part is the reasoning: bins of fifty or so are where the
binomial noise on a rate of 0.8 drops below about 0.06, which with five bins
means several hundred patients. Students who answer "report the counts and a
confidence interval per bin, and do not smooth" have the better answer than
students who name a number.

**The simulation is the teaching, not the forest.** If the room is short of
time, cut Task 2 and keep the noise control. The single most common thing a
student does with their first calibration plot is to narrate a wobble that
sixteen patients cannot support, and the simulation is the only cure. Worth
noting aloud, if someone asks: the top bin on its own does look extreme — a
perfectly calibrated model puts its observed rate between 0.69 and 1.00 ninety
per cent of the time, and we saw 0.63 — but we chose that bin by looking at all
five and picking the worst, which is why the honest test is the one over the
maximum.

**Common failures.** (1) Binning by equal counts instead of equal width and
then comparing the table with the one above; both are defensible and the
numbers differ, so say which you want. (2) In Python, forgetting `.dropna()`
before plotting, which draws a line through an empty bin. (3) Reading the
squashed model's higher Brier score as "a worse model" — it is the same model,
and that is the point of the page. (4) Someone will ask whether you can simply
recalibrate the squashed predictions back; you can, exactly, and Stretch 2 is
where to send them.

**Timing.** The worked example and Task 1 are the floor, 20 minutes. Task 3 and
the three numbered steps are the ceiling and should not be rushed; Task 2 is
the one to drop.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Fix the imbalance, break the probabilities
The booklet has quoted a prevalence near 36% since @sec-first-look and never
resampled it. Try it: keep all 225 `pos` training patients, draw an equal number
of `neg` at random, refit `diabetes ~ glucose` on the balanced 450, and predict
the same 153 test patients.

Nothing happens to the ranking. With one predictor the fitted probability is a
monotone function of glucose whichever rows you fitted on, so the test AUC comes
back as 0.742022 again, to the last digit. Everything happens to the scale: the
mean predicted probability rises from 0.386 to about 0.49, against a prevalence
of 0.359, and the Brier score rises from 0.199 to about 0.212. @sec-thresholds'
threshold of 0.17 now costs 94 or 95 instead of 74, because on the balanced
model 0.17 is a glucose of about 83 rather than about 100 and almost every
patient clears it.

The model is not worse. It is answering a different question — the risk in a
population where diabetes is half as common as it is here is not the risk in
this one — and the threshold was measured on the old scale. Re-minimising the
cost on the new probabilities finds 0.26 or 0.27, and the cost there is 74
again: the same decisions, relabelled. Ask what you would have had to know to
spot this if someone handed you only the resampled model and its AUC.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Put it back
Fit a logistic regression of the outcome on the *log-odds* of the squashed
predictions, using the test set's own outcomes, and look at the slope. This is
Platt scaling, and on a monotone distortion it undoes the damage almost exactly.
Then say why doing it on the test set, as you just did, is not allowed, and what
you would have had to hold back at the start to do it properly.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can build and read a calibration table for a set of predicted
probabilities, that you can say whether its wobbles are larger than the sampling
noise of the test set, and that you know one metric which notices a distortion
that AUC cannot.

**Cannot:** that this model is calibrated. The honest finding is weaker and more
useful: on 153 held-out patients it is not *detectably* miscalibrated, which is
a statement about the test set at least as much as about the model. Nor can you
claim that calibration survives deployment — @sec-shift's covariate shift moves
the case mix, and a model calibrated in development is routinely not calibrated
in the clinic.
